title: Percentage Increase, Decrease, and Change

findings.finding: Recovering the whole from a non-unit fractional percentage requires a reverse method that preceding teaching does not supply.
findings.breakdown: Converting 75% to three quarters still leaves students to recognise that the given amount represents three parts and divide it by three before multiplying by four. Earlier forward calculations and reverse unit-fraction tasks do not model this decision.
findings.checked: Searched all preceding teaching. p20-benchmark and p21-example model forward calculations. p28-q18 can be completed entirely with unit fractions. p28-q20-a supplies a reverse unit-fraction task, and p29-q21 models the same unit-fraction case. Neither supplies the missing divide-by-numerator step needed for the targeted questions.
findings.assumptions: Mental calculation is intended. Fraction arithmetic may be prior knowledge; interpreting a known percentage amount to recover its whole is a new variant here.

repair.proposal: Before p28-q20 add: '75% of a number is 45. Since 75% = 3/4, three equal parts total 45. One part = 45 ÷ 3 = 15. The whole = 15 × 4 = 60.' Follow with: '80% of a number is 40. Four parts total 40; one part = ___; five parts = ___.' Answers: 10, 50.

findings.doneWhen: Students have seen and completed the reverse non-unit-fraction method before using it independently.

findings.finding: Identical complete numerical tasks recur across separate practice sets without a stated retrieval or comparison purpose linking the copies.
findings.breakdown: The repeated tasks supply no fresh calculation. Several belong to useful local comparisons, so replacing isolated values would damage those comparisons; the replacement must preserve each affected group.
findings.checked: Compared complete prompts, including inherited instructions. Confirmed the repeated tasks named in c4. Retained the deliberate interchange comparison in p23-q5-d/e and the notation comparison in p24-q9. Checked replacement values against the supplied tasks: the original proposal would introduce further duplicates, including 5% of 160 and 10% of 50, and would separate the quarter/three-quarter pair in p25-q10-d/e.
findings.assumptions: No additional retrieval purpose is supplied outside the provided material. Related parts are preserved together.

repair.proposal: Make these replacements, leaving other copies unchanged. p25-q10-d/e: 25% and 75% of 44 = 11 and 33; this also removes the duplication with p27-q17-c2-i, which can remain unchanged. p23-q5-f/g/h: 10%, 20% and 5% of 140 = 14, 28 and 7. p25-q10-g: 5% of 180 = 9. p25-q10-m: 5% of 200 = 10. p28-q19-e/f/g: 10%, 5% and 15% of 220 = 22, 11 and 33. p28-q19-a/b/c/d: 10% of 70, 10% of 72, 30% of 70 and 30% of 72 = 7, 7.2, 21 and 21.6. p23-q5-o: 10% of 260 = 26, preserving the complete fixed-whole sequence in p24-q7. p25-q10-b: 20% of 65 = 13. p27-q17-c3-c/d: 45% of 40 and 40% of 45 = 18 and 18. p27-q17-c1-c/d/e: 25% of 160, 25% of 640 and 75% of 160 = 40, 160 and 120. p27-q17-c3-j/k: 3% and 103% of 140 = 4.2 and 144.2. p27-q17-c3-a: 24% of 25 = 6.

findings.doneWhen: Each confirmed repeated calculation has distinct values across its unnecessary copies, while the local scaling, interchange, complementary-percentage and addition-of-a-whole comparisons remain intact.

findings.finding: Use part c to expose why equal percentage increases and decreases do not cancel.
findings.breakdown: The second percentage acts on the increased amount, making the changing reference amount visible.
findings.checked: Part c increases 120 by 20% to 144. A subsequent 20% decrease removes 28.8 and leaves 115.2. Both operations are taught before this exercise.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up using mental strategies from this topic.

repair.proposal: Append: '(g) Decrease your answer to part c by 20%.' Answer: 115.2. '(h) Explain why this does not return to 120.' Expected answer: the increase was 20% of 120, or 24, whereas the decrease is 20% of 144, or 28.8.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts compare the two percentage amounts and their different reference amounts.

findings.finding: Extend the mixture question by changing its composition and then restoring the original percentage.
findings.breakdown: Students must update the total mixture as well as the amount of Chemical A, reinforcing the denominator decision central to the existing question.
findings.checked: The original mixture contains 40 g of A in 125 g, giving 32%. Adding 40 g of A gives 80/165 × 100 ≈ 48.48%. Adding 85 g of B then gives 80/250 × 100 = 32%. These require only the topic's taught percentage-of-another method.
findings.assumptions: Calculator use follows this topic's explicit instructions.

repair.proposal: Append follow-up parts: '(a) Another 40 g of Chemical A is added to the original mixture. What percentage of the mixture is now Chemical A? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.' Answer: 48.48%. '(b) Then another 85 g of Chemical B is added. What percentage of the mixture is now Chemical A?' Answer: 32%. '(c) Explain why the percentage in part b equals the original percentage.' Expected answer: both chemical amounts have doubled, so Chemical A remains the same fraction of the total.

findings.doneWhen: Each part asks one question and students compare the changing numerator and total.

findings.finding: Parts g and h repeat the identical whole task, 'Find 160% of 35', without a stated instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The second copy adds no calculation or distinction to the surrounding comparison of percentage operations.
findings.checked: Compared the complete prompts and surrounding parts d–i. The comparison with increasing 35 by 60% requires only one copy; no instruction gives the second copy a retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.assumptions: Parts g and h are separate practice tasks.

repair.proposal: Keep part g. Change part h to 'Find 160% of 60.' Answer: 96.

findings.doneWhen: Part h retains the percentage-of structure with different values.

findings.finding: Hold dollar profit fixed while increasing cost price to expose the effect of the reference amount on percentage profit.
findings.breakdown: Equal dollar profits produce smaller percentage profits as cost price rises.
findings.checked: The proposed original middle row repeats existing row 5. Revised values avoid that duplication. Profits of $6 on costs of $15, $30 and $60 give 40%, 20% and 10%. All calculations use p56-calculating.
findings.assumptions: Further rows use the existing table instruction and columns.

repair.proposal: After row 8 add the single instruction 'Predict how the percentage profit will change before calculating.' Add rows with cost/selling prices $15/$21, $30/$36 and $60/$66. Expected entries: $6 profit, 40% profit; $6 profit, 20% profit; $6 profit, 10% profit. Follow with an unpatterned row $40/$50: $10 profit, 25% profit. Cost price varies while dollar profit stays at $6 throughout the three-row run.

findings.doneWhen: The three-row run and unpatterned follow-up appear under the existing table instruction, with only the prediction line added.

findings.finding: Follow the investment comparison by finding a selling price that gives equal percentage profit.
findings.breakdown: Students connect percentage profit with the previously taught calculation of an increased amount.
findings.checked: Investment A earns (650 − 500)/500 × 100 = 30%. A 30% profit on Investment B's $800 cost requires a selling price of 800 × 1.30 = $1040. Both methods are available by the end of this topic.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up to the existing investment question.

repair.proposal: Label the existing question part a and append '(b) What selling price would give Investment B the same percentage profit as Investment A?' Answer: $1040.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing investments and asks for the concrete selling price.
